course.title: Earth Science & Geology
course.description: A hands-on tour of the solid Earth — how our planet is built, how its plates move, how rocks and minerals form, and how quakes, volcanoes, water, and deep time reshape the surface. Structure adapted from CK-12 Earth Science (CC BY-NC 3.0).

questions.prompt: The rigid outer shell of Earth that is broken into moving plates is the…
questions.explanation: The lithosphere (crust + rigid uppermost mantle) forms the tectonic plates — see 'Earth's structure & plate tectonics'.

questions.prompt: Igneous rock forms when…
options: heat and pressure change an existing rock
questions.explanation: Igneous = from cooled magma or lava — see 'Rocks & the rock cycle'.

questions.prompt: A naturally occurring solid with a definite chemical composition and orderly crystal structure is a…
questions.explanation: That is the definition of a mineral — see 'Minerals'.

questions.prompt: The point inside Earth where an earthquake's rupture begins is the…
questions.explanation: The focus is underground; the epicenter is the point on the surface above it — see 'Earthquakes & volcanoes'.

questions.prompt: The breakdown of rock into smaller pieces without moving it is called…
questions.explanation: Weathering breaks rock in place; erosion transports it — see 'Weathering, erosion & the water cycle'.

questions.prompt: Most of Earth's fresh liquid and frozen water, aside from oceans, is stored as…
questions.explanation: Glaciers and ice caps hold the majority of fresh water — see 'the water cycle'.

questions.prompt: The principle that in undisturbed layers the oldest rock lies at the bottom is called…
questions.explanation: The law of superposition orders sedimentary layers by age — see 'Earth's history & geologic time'.

questions.prompt: Two tectonic plates pulling apart form a…
questions.explanation: Divergent boundaries (like mid-ocean ridges) spread apart as new crust forms — see 'plate tectonics'.

lessons.title: Earth's structure and plate tectonics
lessons.grammar_note: Lithosphere = rigid plate; asthenosphere = the soft layer it slides on.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Name Earth's internal layers and explain how plate motion is driven. Warm-up: from the diagnostic, which layer is broken into moving plates?

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: Earth is layered by density. The thin *crust* rests on the thick, mostly solid *mantle*; below that is a molten *outer core* and a solid *inner core* of iron and nickel. Mechanically, the cold rigid outer layer is the *lithosphere*, and it rides on the hotter, slowly flowing *asthenosphere*. The lithosphere is cracked into *tectonic plates*. Heat escaping from the interior drives slow convection in the mantle, and the plates move a few centimeters a year. Plates meet at three boundary types: *divergent* (spreading apart, new crust forms at mid-ocean ridges), *convergent* (colliding, where one plate may *subduct* beneath another), and *transform* (grinding sideways past each other).

sections.heading: Worked examples
sections.text: Example 1: The Mid-Atlantic Ridge is a divergent boundary — magma rises, cools, and adds new ocean floor, pushing the Americas and Africa apart. Example 2: Off South America the dense oceanic Nazca plate subducts beneath the continental plate, melting at depth and feeding the Andes volcanoes while raising the mountains. Example 3: California's San Andreas Fault is a transform boundary — the Pacific and North American plates slide past one another, storing strain that is later released as earthquakes.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: Classify each boundary: (1) the East African Rift where the continent is tearing open, (2) the Himalayas where India collides with Asia, (3) the San Andreas Fault, (4) a mid-ocean ridge adding new seafloor. Answers: (1) divergent, (2) convergent (continent-continent collision), (3) transform, (4) divergent.

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: thinking the crust and lithosphere are the same — the lithosphere includes the crust plus the rigid top of the mantle. Mistake: picturing plates floating on a fully liquid mantle (the asthenosphere flows slowly but is solid rock). Exit: (a) What soft layer do plates slide on? (b) At which boundary type is new crust created? Answers: the asthenosphere; divergent.

lessons.title: Rocks and the rock cycle
lessons.grammar_note: Three families: igneous (cooled melt), sedimentary (cemented bits), metamorphic (changed by heat/pressure).

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Identify the three rock families and trace how one becomes another. Warm-up: what kind of rock forms when molten material cools?

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: A *rock* is a solid mixture of one or more minerals. There are three families. *Igneous* rock forms when *magma* (underground) or *lava* (at the surface) cools and crystallizes — slow cooling underground makes large crystals (granite), fast cooling at the surface makes tiny ones (basalt). *Sedimentary* rock forms when weathered fragments are deposited, compacted, and cemented in layers (sandstone), or when minerals precipitate from water (limestone). *Metamorphic* rock forms when an existing rock is reshaped by heat and pressure without melting (shale becomes slate; limestone becomes marble). The *rock cycle* links them: any rock can be melted, weathered into sediment, or metamorphosed and thus become another type.

sections.heading: Worked examples
sections.text: Example 1: Lava erupts from a volcano, cools within days, and forms fine-grained basalt (igneous). Example 2: A granite cliff is weathered into sand; the sand is buried, compacted, and cemented into sandstone (sedimentary). Example 3: That sandstone is dragged deep into a mountain-building collision, where heat and pressure recrystallize it into quartzite (metamorphic) — one rock passing through all three stations of the cycle.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: Name the family: (1) marble carved from heated limestone, (2) basalt from a lava flow, (3) shale made of compacted mud, (4) granite with large interlocking crystals, (5) slate split from pressurized shale. Answers: (1) metamorphic, (2) igneous, (3) sedimentary, (4) igneous, (5) metamorphic.

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: assuming metamorphic rock has melted — it changes in the solid state; melting would make it igneous instead. Mistake: thinking the rock cycle has a fixed order (any rock can become any other). Exit: (a) Which family forms from cooled melt? (b) Fast cooling makes crystals that are large or small? Answers: igneous; small.

lessons.title: Minerals: the building blocks of rock
lessons.grammar_note: Minerals are identified by properties: hardness, streak, luster, cleavage.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: State what makes something a mineral and use physical properties to identify one. Warm-up: is a rock the same thing as a mineral?

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: A *mineral* is a naturally occurring, inorganic solid with a definite chemical composition and an orderly internal *crystal structure*. Rocks are mixtures of minerals, so minerals are the building blocks. Because each mineral's atoms are arranged the same way, minerals show consistent physical properties used to identify them: *hardness* (resistance to scratching, ranked 1–10 on the *Mohs scale*), *streak* (the color of the powder left on a tile), *luster* (how the surface reflects light — metallic or non-metallic), *cleavage* (the tendency to break along flat planes), and *color*. Because color can be misleading, geologists rely more on streak, hardness, and cleavage.

sections.heading: Worked examples
sections.text: Example 1: Talc scratches with a fingernail (Mohs 1) while diamond (Mohs 10) scratches everything — so a mineral that scratches glass but not quartz sits around Mohs 6. Example 2: Pyrite and gold both look golden, but pyrite leaves a greenish-black streak and gold leaves a yellow streak — streak tells 'fool's gold' from the real thing. Example 3: Mica peels into thin flat sheets because it has one direction of perfect cleavage, while quartz breaks along curved surfaces (fracture, not cleavage).

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: Which property is being used? (1) rubbing a mineral on a tile to see the powder color, (2) trying to scratch it with a steel nail, (3) noticing it splits into flat sheets, (4) seeing a shiny metal-like shine. Answers: (1) streak, (2) hardness, (3) cleavage, (4) luster.

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: trusting color alone (many minerals share colors and impurities change them). Mistake: calling ice or coal 'not a mineral' incorrectly — natural ice qualifies, but coal, being organic, does not. Exit: (a) Which is more reliable, color or streak? (b) What scale ranks hardness? Answers: streak; the Mohs scale.

questions.prompt: Tectonic plates move mainly because of…
options: convection of heat in the mantle
questions.explanation: Mantle convection driven by internal heat drives plate motion.

questions.prompt: New oceanic crust is created at a…
questions.explanation: Mid-ocean ridges are divergent boundaries where magma forms new seafloor.

questions.prompt: Granite has large crystals because it…
questions.explanation: Slow underground cooling allows large crystals to grow.

questions.prompt: Limestone changed by heat and pressure into marble is now a … rock.
questions.explanation: Metamorphism reshapes rock in the solid state.

questions.prompt: To tell real gold from pyrite, the best single test is…
questions.explanation: Streak color reliably distinguishes them; gold streaks yellow, pyrite greenish-black.

questions.prompt: The lithosphere slides on the layer directly beneath it, the…
questions.explanation: The rigid lithosphere moves over the slowly flowing asthenosphere.

lessons.title: Earthquakes and volcanoes
lessons.grammar_note: Focus = underground start point; epicenter = the surface point above it.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Explain what causes earthquakes and volcanoes and connect both to plate boundaries. Warm-up: what is the difference between an earthquake's focus and its epicenter?

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: An *earthquake* happens when stress along a *fault* is suddenly released as rock slips, sending out *seismic waves*. The slip starts at the *focus* (or hypocenter) underground; the point on the surface directly above is the *epicenter*. Waves are recorded on a *seismograph*, and their size is reported as *magnitude*. A *volcano* forms where *magma* reaches the surface. Magma forms mainly where plates diverge (rising mantle melts) or where one plate subducts and releases water that lowers the melting point of the mantle above. Thin, runny magma produces gentle flows; thick, gas-rich magma traps pressure and can erupt explosively. Both hazards cluster along plate boundaries — the 'Ring of Fire' around the Pacific rings a chain of subduction zones.

sections.heading: Worked examples
sections.text: Example 1: Strain builds on the San Andreas transform fault for decades, then rock slips in seconds — the released energy radiates as seismic waves felt as shaking. Example 2: At the Cascades subduction zone, the descending plate releases water, melting rock above and feeding stratovolcanoes like Mount St. Helens, whose thick magma erupted explosively in 1980. Example 3: In Hawaii, far from a boundary, a mantle *hotspot* melts through the moving plate, and its thin basaltic lava builds broad, gently sloped shield volcanoes with mostly calm eruptions.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: Answer each: (1) Is the epicenter above or below the focus? (2) Which magma erupts more explosively, thin runny or thick gas-rich? (3) Name the boundary type that both subducts a plate and builds volcanoes. (4) Does most seismic and volcanic activity occur at plate edges or plate centers? Answers: (1) above, (2) thick gas-rich, (3) convergent (subduction), (4) at plate edges.

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: swapping focus and epicenter (the epicenter is the surface point). Mistake: thinking all volcanoes explode violently — shield volcanoes with runny lava mostly do not. Exit: (a) What instrument records seismic waves? (b) What does subducting water do to the mantle above it? Answers: a seismograph; it lowers the melting point, causing melting.

lessons.title: Weathering, erosion, and the water cycle
lessons.grammar_note: Weathering breaks rock in place; erosion moves the pieces; deposition drops them.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Distinguish weathering, erosion, and deposition, and place them inside the water cycle. Warm-up: does weathering move rock, or just break it?

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: *Weathering* breaks rock into smaller pieces where it sits. *Mechanical* weathering breaks rock physically — water freezing in cracks, roots prying, or heating and cooling. *Chemical* weathering changes rock's minerals — acidic rainwater slowly dissolving limestone, or iron rusting. *Erosion* is the transport of the loosened material by water, wind, ice, or gravity, and *deposition* is where that material finally settles. Water powers most of this, and it is recycled through the *water cycle*: solar heat drives *evaporation* from oceans and lakes, vapor rises and *condenses* into clouds, *precipitation* falls as rain or snow, and water returns by runoff to rivers and by *infiltration* into groundwater. Most of Earth's fresh water is locked in glaciers and ice caps.

sections.heading: Worked examples
sections.text: Example 1: Water seeps into a rock crack, freezes overnight, expands about 9%, and wedges the rock apart — mechanical (frost) weathering. Example 2: Mildly acidic rainwater dissolves limestone underground over millennia, carving caves and sinkholes — chemical weathering. Example 3: A river weathers upstream cliffs, erodes and carries the sediment downstream, and deposits it as a fan-shaped delta where the current slows at the sea — weathering, erosion, and deposition in one system.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: Weathering, erosion, or deposition? (1) frost cracking a boulder, (2) a glacier carrying rock debris downhill, (3) sand settling to form a beach, (4) acid rain dissolving a marble statue, (5) wind lifting desert dust into the air, (6) a river dropping silt on a floodplain. Answers: (1) weathering, (2) erosion, (3) deposition, (4) weathering, (5) erosion, (6) deposition.

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: using 'weathering' and 'erosion' as synonyms — weathering breaks rock in place, erosion carries it away. Mistake: thinking most fresh water is in rivers and lakes (it is mostly frozen in ice). Exit: (a) Which process transports the broken pieces? (b) What drives evaporation in the water cycle? Answers: erosion; energy from the Sun.

items.translation: Earth's rigid outer shell (crust plus rigid upper mantle) that is broken into tectonic plates
items.example: The lithosphere slides slowly over the softer asthenosphere beneath it.

items.translation: the process in which one tectonic plate sinks beneath another at a convergent boundary
items.example: Subduction of an oceanic plate can build a chain of volcanoes.

items.translation: the continual process by which rocks change among igneous, sedimentary, and metamorphic forms
items.example: In the rock cycle, sediment can be buried and cemented into sedimentary rock.

items.translation: a natural, inorganic solid with a definite composition and orderly crystal structure
items.example: Quartz is a common mineral identified by its hardness and fracture.

items.translation: the point on Earth's surface directly above an earthquake's underground focus
items.example: Shaking is usually strongest near the epicenter.

items.translation: the framework that divides Earth's 4.6-billion-year history into eons, eras, and periods
items.example: The geologic time scale places the dinosaurs in the Mesozoic Era.

questions.prompt: The underground point where an earthquake begins is the…
questions.explanation: The focus (hypocenter) is underground; the epicenter is above it.

questions.prompt: Thick, gas-rich magma tends to produce eruptions that are…
questions.explanation: Trapped gas in viscous magma causes explosive eruptions.

questions.prompt: Frost wedging, where freezing water splits rock, is an example of…
questions.explanation: It breaks rock physically without changing its chemistry.

questions.prompt: The transport of weathered material by water, wind, or ice is…
questions.explanation: Erosion moves the loosened pieces; deposition then settles them.

questions.prompt: In undisturbed sedimentary layers, the oldest layer is…
questions.explanation: The law of superposition: lower layers were deposited first.

questions.prompt: Most of Earth's fresh water is stored as…
questions.explanation: Ice caps and glaciers hold the majority of fresh water.

lessons.title: Applied project: explain the geology of a place you know

sections.heading: The task
sections.text: Choose a real place you know — a hill, coastline, riverbank, quarry, canyon, or even a road cut you pass often. Write a short account (about 200–300 words) explaining its geology using the ideas from this course. You are not collecting new data; you are reading the landscape with a geologist's eye.

sections.heading: Milestones
sections.text: 1) Describe the landform and any visible rock or sediment (its color, layering, hardness). 2) Propose which rock family it likely belongs to and why. 3) Explain at least one process that shaped it — plate motion, volcanism, weathering, erosion, or deposition. 4) Estimate its relative age using a clue such as layer order, erosion, or fossils, and say what you would look at to test your guess.

sections.heading: Self-check rubric
sections.text: ✔ You named a specific place and described what is actually visible. ✔ You classified the rock or sediment and justified it. ✔ You tied the landform to at least one named Earth-science process. ✔ You reasoned about relative age and how you would check it. If all four are true, you have explained a real landscape the way an Earth scientist would.
